title: Acute severe ulcerative colitis
subject: gastroenterology
setting: Emergency department, gastroenterology ward, with colorectal surgery
summary: Truelove and Witts severe colitis: admit, exclude infection (C. difficile, CMV), start IV methylprednisolone 60 mg/day or hydrocortisone 100 mg 3 to 4 times daily with LMWH prophylaxis, assess on day 3 and give infliximab or ciclosporin rescue to non-responders, with early surgical review.

sections.title: Recognise ASUC
items: Truelove and Witts: 6 or more bloody stools a day plus at least one sign of systemic toxicity: pulse above 90/min, temperature above 37.8 °C, Hb below 10.5 g/dL or ESR above 30 mm/h.
Admit every patient with ASUC; it is a medical emergency with a substantial colectomy risk. Involve gastroenterology and colorectal surgery from admission.
Toxic megacolon: colonic dilatation (transverse colon above 5.5 cm) with systemic toxicity; perforation risk is high.
In India, exclude infective colitis that mimics or complicates UC, including amoebic colitis, bacillary dysentery and intestinal tuberculosis.

sections.title: Admission bundle (day 1)
items: Bloods: CBC, CRP, ESR, urea, electrolytes including potassium and magnesium, LFT with albumin. Stool culture and Clostridioides difficile testing in every patient (ACG 2025 strong recommendation).
Plain abdominal X-ray for dilatation, mucosal islands or dilated small-bowel loops; CT only if perforation, collection or other complication is suspected.
Flexible sigmoidoscopy within 24 hours (at most 72 hours), with minimal insufflation, to confirm severity and take biopsies for CMV (immunohistochemistry or PCR).
Start IV corticosteroids without delay: methylprednisolone 60 mg/day or hydrocortisone 100 mg 3 to 4 times daily. Higher doses add no benefit.
Pharmacological VTE prophylaxis with LMWH for all patients; it is safe despite rectal bleeding.

IV fluids, correct potassium and magnesium, transfuse if needed; encourage oral or enteral nutrition (no bowel rest or parenteral nutrition). No routine antibiotics unless infection or toxicity is suspected.
Stop NSAIDs, opioids, anticholinergic and antidiarrhoeal drugs; stop a recently started 5-ASA if paradoxical reaction is possible.
Send pre-biologic screening on admission so rescue is not delayed: HBsAg and anti-HBc, HCV, HIV, tuberculosis screen (IGRA and chest X-ray; latent TB is common in India), varicella status.

sections.title: Daily review and day 3 assessment
items: Daily: stool chart (frequency, blood), pulse, temperature, abdominal examination for distension or tenderness, CRP, albumin, potassium and magnesium.
Day 3 of IV steroids (Oxford or Travis criteria): more than 8 stools a day, or 3 to 8 stools with CRP above 45 mg/L, predicts colectomy in about 85%. Start rescue therapy.
Response to IV steroids usually appears in 3 to 5 days; further response after 7 days is unlikely, so do not prolong IV steroids without rescue.
Repeat abdominal X-ray if distension, pain or clinical deterioration develops.

sections.title: Rescue therapy for steroid non-responders
items: Choose infliximab or ciclosporin (similar outcomes in the CySIF and CONSTRUCT trials) based on local experience, prior thiopurine or anti-TNF failure, and serum albumin. Obtain surgical consultation when rescue starts.
Infliximab 5 mg/kg IV at weeks 0, 2 and 6; consider an intensified first dose of 10 mg/kg when serum albumin is below 2.5 g/dL. Maintain remission with infliximab.
Ciclosporin 2 mg/kg/day continuous IV infusion (trough level about 200 to 400 ng/mL), then oral ciclosporin as a bridge to thiopurine (or vedolizumab) maintenance.
Before ciclosporin check BP, creatinine, magnesium and cholesterol; avoid with low magnesium or cholesterol (seizure risk), renal impairment or uncontrolled hypertension.
Tofacitinib or upadacitinib: insufficient data for routine rescue; consider only in highly selected patients when conventional rescue and surgery are contraindicated (BSG 2025).
CMV colitis in a steroid-refractory patient: IV ganciclovir, then oral valganciclovir, for about 14 days; continue colitis treatment and do not delay colectomy.
C. difficile infection: oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin, without stopping colitis therapy.

sections.title: Surgery
items: Emergency colectomy for toxic megacolon, perforation or massive haemorrhage.
Failure of rescue therapy: proceed to colectomy without delay; median time to response in CySIF was 4 to 5 days, and response is judged by about day 7.
Operation of choice: subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy. Prior infliximab or ciclosporin does not increase postoperative complications.
Delayed surgery in ASUC is associated with worse outcomes and higher mortality.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Continuing IV steroids beyond day 5 to 7 in non-responders instead of starting rescue or surgery.
Missing C. difficile or CMV, or infective colitis such as amoebiasis.
Withholding LMWH because of rectal bleeding.
Giving opioids or antidiarrhoeals, which can precipitate toxic megacolon.
Delaying infliximab because TB and hepatitis B screening was not sent on admission.

drugs.name: Methylprednisolone
drugs.dose: 60 mg IV per day (single or divided doses)
drugs.notes: First-line induction; no benefit from higher doses.

drugs.name: Enoxaparin
drugs.notes: VTE prophylaxis for all admitted patients. Reduce the dose if creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min (per product labelling).

drugs.name: Infliximab
drugs.dose: 5 mg/kg IV infusion at weeks 0, 2 and 6
drugs.notes: Consider 10 mg/kg first dose if albumin below 2.5 g/dL. Screen for TB and hepatitis B first.

drugs.name: Ciclosporin
drugs.notes: Target trough about 200 to 400 ng/mL; monitor BP, creatinine, magnesium; bridge to thiopurine.

drugs.name: Oral vancomycin (C. difficile)
drugs.dose: 125 mg orally four times daily for 10 days
drugs.notes: Fidaxomicin 200 mg twice daily for 10 days is an alternative.

drugs.name: Ganciclovir (CMV colitis)
drugs.dose: 5 mg/kg IV every 12 hours, then valganciclovir 900 mg orally twice daily, total about 14 days
drugs.notes: Adjust for renal function; monitor blood counts.

sources.title: ACG Clinical Guideline Update: Ulcerative Colitis in Adults (Rubin et al., Am J Gastroenterol)
Guideline review: 2025 BSG guidelines on inflammatory bowel disease in adults, Part 2: ulcerative colitis (Frontline Gastroenterology)
